Whole garment and intended logo area visible
Rear coverage, seams and leg shape
Angle and scale comparable with other styles
Gusset or pouch lining and attachment
Actual construction visible without misleading retouching
Lace, edge finish, waistband or branding
Focus and lighting reveal the relevant feature

sections.title: Photograph the sample version that the listing describes
paragraphs: Record the model, photographed size, colour and sample approval status before the shoot. If a prototype uses temporary trims or a substitute fabric, keep its images separate from the final product assets. Otherwise an early development photograph can remain on a live page after the garment changes.

Use consistent angles, lighting and framing for comparable catalogue views. Include enough margin to prevent logos or garment edges from being cut off in cards and mobile layouts. Check the actual website crop as well as the original image file.

sections.title: Keep colour and fit representation honest
paragraphs: Use a controlled colour workflow and compare the edited result with the physical reference. Screens and viewing conditions still vary, so photography should not replace physical colour approval for production. Avoid aggressive edits that conceal the texture or make one colourway appear to be a different material.

For worn views, choose a suitable sample size and record styling adjustments. Do not reshape the garment digitally to imply a different cut or erase seams that are present in the supplied product. A close-up can show a lining, but it cannot prove fibre percentages, certification or a tested performance claim.

sections.title: Organise image rights, names and page use
paragraphs: Confirm permission for the intended use of supplier photographs, photographer work and model imagery. Keep original assets with the agreed usage record. If a photograph includes a supplier logo, agree any branding treatment and retain an accurate reference rather than cropping away useful construction details to hide it.

Name delivered files with the style, colour and view, and write alt text describing what the image actually shows. Keep generated concepts separate from evidence of real garments or factory work. Before publishing, verify that each gallery, thumbnail and social preview points to the correct product version.

sections.title: Product-photography questions
paragraphs: Can one front image serve every related style? It should not stand in for different back shapes or construction. Show the exact model and identify any illustrative image clearly.
Do I need a new model shoot for every detail? Flat-lay and inside close-ups can explain many construction questions. Choose the format that makes the actual feature clear.

Can AI imagery replace the sample photos? It can support a clearly identified creative concept, but it should not be presented as proof of the finished product's appearance, fit or manufacturing process.

title: Women's Boyshorts vs Long-Leg Underwear: Buyer Guide
description: Compare cotton boyshorts, women's boxers and long-leg briefs. Use three DIYASI styles to define coverage, leg openings and fit checks before sampling.
coverAlt: Rear view of a pale pink DIYASI DYS214 cotton boyshort showing the back coverage and leg openings
imageCaption: DYS214 provides a boyshort reference. Compare the physical sample with DYS215 and DYS210 to assess waistband height, leg length and back coverage.
intro: Women's boyshorts, boxers and long-leg briefs should be compared by their finished shape, not the name alone. For a private-label collection, decide how much upper-leg and rear coverage the customer wants, where the waistband should sit and how the leg opening should fit. DIYASI's DYS214, DYS215 and DYS210 offer three cotton-spandex starting points. A longer leg does not by itself establish anti-chafing performance, and a high waist does not make a garment shapewear.

sections.title: Compare three cotton silhouettes
paragraphs: All three catalogue examples list 95% combed cotton and 5% spandex, with sizes S to XL. Keeping the listed blend similar makes the shape differences easier to discuss, although fabric weight, finishing and pattern measurements still need confirmation. A shared composition does not mean that the garments fit identically.

Use the exact model number when requesting front, back and side references. The word boxer can describe different garments between suppliers; specifying DYS215 prevents an enquiry for a fitted underwear style from being interpreted as a request for loose sleep shorts.

Regular-rise women's boxer with wide waistband

sections.title: Measure leg coverage instead of estimating from photos
paragraphs: Ask for front rise, back rise, side length, inseam where applicable, and relaxed leg-opening measurements. Mark the measurement endpoints on a drawing. A longer side can result from a higher waist, a longer leg, or both; side length alone cannot tell the buyer which change has been made.

For a fitted leg, record the hem construction and the intended stretch condition used for measurement. Check the same points on each sample laid flat without pulling. Compare the garment with the intended body measurements rather than translating an S or M label from an unrelated brand.

sections.title: Review movement and outer-clothing compatibility
paragraphs: During a fit review, observe the hem after sitting, walking and bending. Record whether it rolls, shifts or creates pressure, and identify the exact location in the feedback. Increasing the leg length is not automatically the correct response: the opening, fabric recovery or seam tension may need attention.

If the garment is intended for wear under trousers or skirts, review it under representative clothing. Record visible hems and waist edges separately from comfort observations. A sample review can guide development, but it is not evidence for a universal no-show or anti-chafing claim.

sections.title: Choose a clear role for each style
paragraphs: A brand might select a boyshort as an alternative to bikini briefs, a wide-waistband boxer for a particular styling direction, and a longer brief for customers requesting additional leg coverage. These are assortment choices to validate with customers, rather than predictions of which silhouette will sell fastest.

Keep the first sample comparison focused on one size reference and an agreed fabric direction. Once the shape is selected, review the required size set and colour allocation. Include the exact model, measurement revisions and intended use in the enquiry so the factory can assess the request.

sections.title: Buyer questions about boyshorts and longer briefs
paragraphs: Are women's boxers always loose? No. The name varies, so compare the actual pattern and finished measurements. DYS215 is a catalogue reference for a women's cotton underwear boxer with a wide waistband.
Will a longer leg stop ride-up? Not necessarily. Leg opening, fit, stretch recovery and movement all affect the result. Request a sample review for the intended wearer and use.
Can DYS210 be sold as compression underwear? Its high waist and extended leg do not establish compression. Any such claim requires a suitable design specification and supporting evidence.

title: V-Waist Underwear: Fit & Measurement Guide for Buyers
description: Specify V-waist underwear using centre-front depth, side height and waistband construction. Compare DIYASI lace and seamless styles before sample approval.
coverAlt: Black DIYASI LS005-142 brief with a V-shaped lace waistband and cotton front panel
imageCaption: The LS005-142 lace waistband shows why a V-waist brief needs separate centre-front and side-height references in a technical specification.
intro: A V-waist underwear brief should define the shape of the waistband separately from rise and rear coverage. Record the centre-front dip, the height at the sides and the back-waist position on a drawing with agreed measurement points. DIYASI's LS005-142 lace brief and DYS301 seamless thong both use a V-shaped waist, while DYS201 offers a low-rise cotton bikini reference. Their shared low-rise direction does not make their waist construction or fit interchangeable.

sections.title: Separate waist shape from the rest of the silhouette
paragraphs: A V-shaped waist describes the front outline. It does not tell you whether the garment is a brief or thong, how much back coverage it provides, or how tightly the waistband fits. Those decisions belong in separate fields of the development brief.

LS005-142 combines a cotton-spandex body with a polyamide-spandex lace waistband. DYS301 uses a polyamide-spandex body with a cotton gusset. Compare their pattern lines and materials together; the visual shape can be similar while the edge finish and stretch behaviour differ.

sections.title: Draw the V before assigning a rise measurement
paragraphs: Mark a consistent horizontal reference line and show the distance to the centre-front waist and both side-waist points. Define how front rise is measured through the garment. Otherwise one reviewer may measure to the low point of the V while another measures to an imagined straight waistband.

Record back rise and side height independently. A request to lower the front does not automatically mean lowering the back or narrowing the side panel. Add a front and back technical drawing with the revised line highlighted so the pattern maker can identify exactly what changes.

sections.title: Review the centre join and the full waistband
paragraphs: For a lace V, inspect the centre join inside and outside. Note symmetry, seam bulk, exposed thread ends and how the lace motif meets at the join. Specify which visual details require approval; do not assume perfect motif matching is included without discussing feasibility and cost.

For either construction, review the waist relaxed and during the agreed fit movements. Check whether the centre lies in the intended position, the sides feel balanced and the back stays stable. Record rolling or gaping at a named point instead of describing the entire waistband as too loose.

sections.title: Carry the shape through the size range
paragraphs: A V that looks balanced on one size may need different grading decisions at the ends of the range. Ask how centre depth, side height and waistband length change between sizes. Review representative size-set samples with the same measurement definitions used for the base size.

Keep each approved drawing and sample under a version number. When requesting a colour or label change later, state whether the V outline remains as approved. This prevents a branding revision from accidentally reopening the fit specification.

sections.title: Common V-waist development questions
paragraphs: Does V-waist mean high-leg? No. Waist outline and leg-opening height are separate design choices and should have separate drawing references.

Can a straight waistband simply be cut into a V? Treat that as a pattern and construction change. The front panel, edge finish and stretch balance need review before the factory can confirm the development work.
Which V-waist style is more comfortable? A product name cannot settle that question. Compare the intended size, coverage and material with physical samples and specific wearer feedback.

title: Men's Briefs vs Trunks: A Private Label Fit Comparison
description: Compare men's briefs, bikini briefs and trunks using DIYASI models. Define leg coverage, rise, pouch and waistband requirements for your sample brief.
coverAlt: Grey DIYASI M008 men's bikini brief showing the low-rise waistband and shaped no-fly front
imageCaption: M008 is the low-rise bikini brief reference in this comparison. M001 and M004 provide a brief and a trunk for reviewing different coverage choices.
intro: The main buying distinction between men's briefs and trunks is the leg silhouette: briefs leave more of the upper leg uncovered, while trunks include short legs. Rise, pouch shape, fly construction and waistband tension remain separate decisions. DIYASI's M001 low-rise brief, M008 low-rise bikini brief and M004 mid-rise trunk let a private-label buyer compare these choices using identifiable catalogue styles. None of the names alone proves support, moisture management or a particular comfort outcome.

sections.title: Use three references to define the intended coverage
paragraphs: The current catalogue lists these styles in S through 3XL. Each describes a polyester-spandex body and modal lining at the pouch or gusset, without publishing exact fibre percentages. Request the final component composition before preparing labels or making a fabric claim.

Keep model numbers attached to the photographs in your shortlist. A generic request for men's briefs can leave the supplier uncertain about side width, leg opening and waistband position. The table gives a starting point; approved measurements determine the order.

sections.title: Measure rise and leg openings separately
paragraphs: For the briefs, request front and back rise, side width and leg-opening measurements with illustrated endpoints. For the trunk, add inseam and hem-opening measurements. Do not use a trunk inseam as a way to describe a brief that has a different leg construction.

Define whether waist and openings are measured relaxed or under an agreed stretch method. A flat width is not a wearer waist circumference. Keep the buyer's body-size chart separate from the finished-garment specification, and use a fit review to assess the relationship between them.

sections.title: Evaluate the pouch independently of leg length
paragraphs: Review pouch depth, lining coverage, seam location and the inside finish on each sample. The length of the outer leg does not establish how much room the pouch provides. Likewise, a no-fly design describes the front opening arrangement rather than a measured support level.

Ask reviewers to identify where pulling or excess fabric occurs while standing and sitting. Keep feedback about the pouch separate from comments on leg hems and the waistband. This allows the factory to propose a targeted pattern change instead of changing the entire size.

sections.title: Plan the first assortment around distinct needs
paragraphs: If a brand is testing demand for less leg coverage, one brief and one trunk can provide a clearer comparison than several similar trunk variations. Use customer evidence to decide the eventual mix. Catalogue breadth is not evidence that every silhouette deserves equal order quantities.

For a fair sample review, use the same intended body-size reference and document the requested colour and waistband direction. Confirm availability, branding changes and quantities separately for each model. A common size label or a similar photograph is not a promise of shared patterns or stock.

sections.title: Questions buyers ask about men's briefs and trunks
paragraphs: Is a bikini brief just a smaller standard brief? Not necessarily. Side width and leg shape may change without the garment belonging to a smaller body-size category. Review the pattern and measurement chart.
Are trunks automatically better for sport? No. Activity-specific performance needs its own design requirements and evidence; short legs alone do not establish suitability.
Can one size chart cover both styles? A body-size guide may be shared if fit development supports it, but finished measurements and grading still need approval for each silhouette.

title: Modal Pouch vs Modal Underwear: Read the Fabric Spec
description: Learn why a modal-lined pouch does not mean an all-modal garment. Review body, lining and waistband specifications using three DIYASI men's styles.
coverAlt: Grey marl DIYASI M003 men's trunk with a shaped front pouch and plain waistband
imageCaption: M003 is listed with a polyester-spandex body and modal pouch lining. The exterior photograph does not establish the fibre percentages of either component.
intro: A modal pouch or modal lining refers to a component of the garment, not necessarily its main body fabric. DIYASI's M003, M005 and M004 Print list polyester and spandex for the body and modal for the pouch or gusset lining. Their public specifications do not provide exact component percentages. Buyers should request a component-level fabric specification before writing product descriptions, approving fibre labels or comparing quotations for an all-modal underwear range.

sections.title: Read the specification by garment component
paragraphs: Start with the outer body, then identify the pouch lining, gusset, waistband and any other separate material. A title may highlight one feature while the material table describes several. Record both the location and the fibre blend so a marketing phrase cannot be mistaken for the composition of the whole garment.

The three examples below are useful for learning this distinction, but they are not controlled fabric-performance comparisons. Their patterns and finishes differ, and the published information does not include laboratory results.

sections.title: Request evidence that identifies the actual material
paragraphs: Ask the supplier for the bill of materials and relevant composition records tied to the proposed fabric references. If laboratory verification is required, agree which components and production material the test will cover. A report for an unrelated fabric cannot verify the composition of your order.

Keep the material codes on the sample card and quotation. When the factory proposes a substitute, record what changes and which approvals must be repeated. A visually similar grey body fabric or soft lining may have a different composition, weight or finish.

sections.title: Separate fibre identity from comfort claims
paragraphs: Modal identifies a fibre type; it does not by itself establish the finished garment's support, cooling, moisture management or durability. The lining area, fabric construction, seams and fit all contribute to the wearing experience. Describe the confirmed component accurately and evaluate any additional claim on its own evidence.

Review the inside of the sample as well as the exterior. Check lining coverage, attachment and seam position, then assess the garment under the intended wear and care conditions. Record observations rather than assigning a performance level from the fibre name.

sections.title: Keep recycled-material options specific to the order
paragraphs: M005's source information mentions a recycled-polyester option. That is a direction for discussion, not proof that every M005 sample or order contains recycled material. Ask which component is involved, what proportion is proposed and which traceability or certification documents apply to the actual supply.

Use approved composition and documentation when preparing consumer labels and product copy for the target market. Until the final material is confirmed, the accurate working description is a polyester-spandex body with modal pouch lining, with exact percentages pending confirmation.

sections.title: Common questions about modal-lined underwear
paragraphs: Does modal pouch mean 100% modal underwear? No. It identifies a location in the garment; even the exact lining composition needs confirmation when percentages are not supplied.
Can I replace the body fabric with modal? That is a development request. Fabric behaviour, pattern, construction, cost and minimum quantities need review before a new sample can be approved.
Can an exterior photo confirm a modal lining? No. Inspect the inside and request material records. A photograph can show construction but cannot establish fibre composition.

title: Underwear Tech Pack: Measurements, Materials & Revisions
description: Build an underwear tech pack with illustrated measuring points, component materials, artwork placement and a revision log for consistent sample development.
coverAlt: Pale pink DIYASI DYS223 cotton brief showing the front panel, waistband and finished leg edges
imageCaption: DYS223 is one possible catalogue starting point for a technical pack. The pack must record the buyer's approved measurements and changes rather than relying on a photograph alone.
intro: An underwear tech pack is the controlled specification used to develop and reproduce a garment. Include a style reference, front and back drawings, component materials, measuring points, target dimensions, tolerances, artwork placement and revision history. A quotation brief explains what you want to source; the technical pack records what the sample and production garment must match. Start with an identifiable DIYASI model, then show every requested change instead of assuming the catalogue photograph contains the full specification.

sections.title: Give every page the same style and version reference
paragraphs: Put your internal style code, supplier model, version number and issue date on the document. Name the intended size range and base sample size. Keep drawings, measurement sheets, artwork and comments under the same revision so the factory does not combine a new drawing with an old size table.

For example, DYS223 identifies a cotton brief, DYS301 a V-waist seamless thong and M005 a men's boxer with modal pouch lining. These references narrow the starting point but do not replace a specification for custom material, fit or branding.

sections.title: Make each measurement reproducible
paragraphs: Assign a point-of-measure code to waist width, front rise, back rise, side height, leg opening and relevant gusset dimensions. Add inseam for styles with legs. Draw the endpoints and state whether the garment is measured flat, relaxed or under an agreed stretch method.

Keep body measurements separate from finished-garment measurements. Specify whether a number represents a half width or a full circumference, and use one unit system throughout. Agree practical tolerances with the factory for each important point instead of applying an unexplained universal allowance.

sections.title: Specify components and construction together
paragraphs: List the body, gusset or pouch lining, waistband, thread, labels and other trims separately. DYS301's polyamide-spandex body and cotton gusset are different components; M005's modal lining does not describe its entire body fabric. Leave unknown percentages marked for confirmation rather than filling them by guesswork.

Use close-up callouts for edge finishes, joins and attachment methods that matter to the design. If a catalogue sample is the construction reference, identify it by model and sample version. A request for a softer edge should still explain where the change is needed and how it will be reviewed.

sections.title: Turn sample feedback into a controlled revision
paragraphs: Record the measured sample value beside the target and add an annotated photograph where useful. Separate fit comments from material, workmanship and artwork issues. State the requested correction and whether it requires another sample, a measurement report or another agreed form of verification.

Issue one consolidated revision after resolving conflicting comments. Keep superseded files for traceability, but clearly identify the current version. Approval should refer to that version and the corresponding physical sample, not an isolated message saying that the garment looks good.

sections.title: Tech-pack questions for first-time underwear buyers
paragraphs: Do I need a complete pack to make an initial enquiry? No. A model shortlist and a clear brief can start the discussion. The technical details should be resolved before the relevant development and production approvals.
Can I copy another brand's size labels? Size labels do not supply a measurement specification. Define your intended customer measurements and develop the fit with the factory.
Does a tech pack eliminate sampling? No. It makes the request measurable; samples show whether the proposed materials and construction deliver the intended result.

title: Underwear Colour Approval: Lab Dips, Trims & Bulk Shades
description: Plan underwear colour approval across cotton, polyamide and lace. Define physical colour standards, lab-dip feedback and bulk-shade checks before ordering.
coverAlt: Pale neutral DIYASI DYS202 cotton bikini brief with a plain waistband and matching body fabric
imageCaption: DYS202 illustrates a plain cotton colour direction. Screen images are useful for shortlisting, while physical material references are needed for final shade approval.
intro: Approve an underwear colour on the actual material and under agreed viewing conditions, then carry that reference through trims and bulk fabric. A lab dip is a small dyed sample used to review a proposed shade; it is not approval of the finished production garment. For a range spanning DIYASI cotton, lace and polyamide styles, identify each component that must match and decide whether the goal is a close colour match or an intentional tonal relationship.

sections.title: Create one colour brief with separate material approvals
paragraphs: Provide a physical colour standard or an agreed colour-system reference, its edition where relevant, and the intended fabric. A screenshot or hexadecimal colour can communicate a direction, but screen settings and photography make it an unreliable final dyeing standard.

DYS202 lists a cotton-spandex body, LS006 combines cotton-spandex with polyamide-spandex lace, and DYS323 uses a polyamide-spandex body with a cotton gusset. These components can look different even when developed towards the same colour reference.

sections.title: Make lab-dip feedback specific
paragraphs: Assign an identifier to each dip and compare it with the standard under the agreed lighting. Record whether it is too light, dark, red, yellow or blue rather than sending a photograph with only a request to improve the colour. Keep the physical reference and the feedback tied to the same version.

If the product will be viewed under different light sources, agree which ones matter to the review. Two materials may appear to match under one light and differ under another, a phenomenon known as metamerism. Ask the supplier how this will be assessed for the chosen materials.

sections.title: Approve a component set before judging the garment
paragraphs: Place the body fabric, lace, elastic, thread and labels together on a named approval card. Review the components in their intended orientation and, where relevant, in a sewn sample. Surface texture, transparency and stretch can change how the combination appears.

A shade approval is separate from a colourfastness requirement. If resistance to washing, rubbing or staining is needed, agree the test method and acceptance criteria for the actual material or garment. A visually accepted dip does not demonstrate that those tests have passed.

sections.title: Connect the approved dip to bulk production
paragraphs: Ask how the first bulk fabric will be compared with the approved standard and how dye lots will be identified. Agree whether a bulk cutting or production-material sample needs buyer approval before cutting. Keep a retained reference on both sides where practical.

For reorders, reference the approved physical standard and the relevant previous lot rather than asking for the same beige again. Material changes, finishing changes and different dye lots should trigger the checks agreed in your colour-control plan. Confirm custom-colour quantities and timing in the quotation.

sections.title: Colour-approval questions
paragraphs: Can one dip approve both cotton and polyamide? It can communicate a shared target, but each material needs its own approval reference. Their surfaces and dyeing behaviour differ.
Does a colour code guarantee an exact match? No. The material, finish, viewing conditions and agreed tolerance all matter. Confirm what will count as an acceptable result.
Is a stock-colour sample the same as a custom-colour approval? No. Record whether the order uses an existing colour or requires new colour development, and identify the relevant physical standard.

title: Underwear Wash Review: Shrinkage, Recovery & Appearance
description: Create a repeatable underwear wash review. Record measurements, dimensional change, edge condition and appearance using cotton, polyamide and men's samples.
coverAlt: Purple DIYASI DYS206 cotton bikini brief with stitched waist and leg edges
imageCaption: DYS206 is a cotton-spandex reference for planning measurements before and after washing. This product photograph is not a wash-test result.
intro: A useful underwear wash review compares identified samples before and after a documented care procedure. Record the same measuring points, drying method, cycle count and appearance checks each time, with an unwashed reference for comparison. Use the results to resolve the product specification and care instructions. The process below is a buyer planning checklist, not a claim that DIYASI's example products have passed a particular laboratory standard or achieved a stated shrinkage result.

sections.title: Agree the procedure before washing samples
paragraphs: Identify the model, size, colour, fabric reference and sample version. Agree the intended wash and drying conditions, number of cycles, measurement timing and acceptance criteria with the supplier. If a retailer or target market requires a formal method, arrange the appropriate laboratory work instead of treating an informal home wash as certification.

Keep an unwashed control and record the starting condition of every tested garment. Lay samples flat without pulling when taking relaxed measurements, and use the same method and conditioning period before and after the wash sequence. Otherwise differences in handling can be mistaken for material changes.

Change at each identical measurement point

Visible fading, staining, pilling or distortion
Agreed fit observations and stretch procedure

sections.title: Calculate dimensional change consistently
paragraphs: One clear reporting convention is dimensional change (%) = (after measurement minus before measurement) / before measurement x 100. Under this convention a negative result indicates a reduction. State the convention on the report so it is not confused with a shrinkage percentage expressed as a positive number.

For an illustrative calculation only, a point measuring 30.0 cm before and 29.4 cm after has a dimensional change of -2.0%. This is not a measured DIYASI result or a recommended acceptance limit. Agree the permitted change for each important point according to the product requirements.

sections.title: Choose checks that match the construction
paragraphs: DYS206 is a cotton-spandex bikini with finished edges. DYS314 has a polyamide-spandex body, laser-cut edges and a stitched cotton gusset. M007 is a men's boxer brief with a polyester-spandex body and modal lining. Each calls for attention to different joins, openings and component relationships.

Check the garment as a whole as well as its measurements. A waist can remain within dimensional tolerance while the finish becomes uneven; a body fabric can look unchanged while a lining or seam distorts. If testing a bonded style from the wider range, include its bond condition in the agreed review.

sections.title: Keep recovery and colourfastness evidence distinct
paragraphs: A wash review alone does not quantify stretch recovery. If recovery matters, define the extension, load or method, repetitions and recovery time with the supplier or laboratory. A photograph of fabric being stretched cannot replace that measurement.

Likewise, casual observation of colour after washing is different from a specified colourfastness test. Record the method used and its limitations. Where a change fails the agreed requirement, identify the affected material or construction, revise the sample and repeat the relevant check before approval.

sections.title: Questions about wash approval
paragraphs: Is there one acceptable shrinkage percentage for all underwear? No universal limit is supplied here. The buyer and supplier need an agreed requirement appropriate to the garment and test method.
Can a fabric test replace a garment wash review? Fabric results are useful, but the finished garment includes seams, trims and multiple components that may behave differently together.

Should every colour be tested identically? Agree a testing plan based on the materials, colourways and applicable requirements. Do not assume evidence from one sample automatically covers every variant.

title: Underwear Size-Set Samples: A Grading Review Checklist
description: Check an underwear size set before bulk production. Compare finished measurements, grade increments and fit across sizes using real DIYASI catalogue examples.
coverAlt: Light grey DIYASI DYS219 cotton brief showing its high waist and high-cut leg openings
imageCaption: DYS219 lists sizes XXS through 2XL. A catalogue size range is a starting point for planning, while the final graded measurements need sample approval.
intro: A size-set review checks whether an approved underwear design has been translated consistently across its intended sizes. Compare the finished measurements with the grading table, review the fit at selected sizes and record corrections before production. It is a different task from converting US or EU size labels. DIYASI's DYS219, DYS225 and DYS214 illustrate why the size range and grading should be approved for each silhouette rather than copied from another garment carrying the same size letter.

sections.title: Confirm which sizes belong to each model
paragraphs: DYS219 is listed from XXS to 2XL, DYS225 from S to 2XL and DYS214 from S to XL. These catalogue ranges are not confirmation of current stock or a guarantee that the same labelled size has the same measurements in every model.

Agree the actual range for your order, the base size already approved and which sizes must be supplied for review. Where the range is extended beyond the existing pattern, ask what additional development and fit work is needed rather than assuming a new label creates a finished size.
rows: XXS, XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL
Waist height, high-leg shape and back coverage
Front coverage, back width and gusset position
Leg opening, side coverage and hem position

sections.title: Read the grading table by measurement point
paragraphs: For every point of measure, list the target for each size and the difference between adjacent sizes. Waist width, rise, side height and leg opening do not necessarily use the same increment. Ask the pattern team to explain any change in grading direction at the ends of the range.

Use the same measuring diagrams, units and relaxed or stretched conditions as the base-size approval. Keep the body-size chart beside the garment table without merging the two. A garment's flat waist width cannot be compared directly with a customer's full body circumference.

sections.title: Inspect samples for measurement and fit
paragraphs: Identify each physical sample by style, size and version, then record actual values against targets and agreed tolerances. Check both sides where symmetry matters. Record a measurement deviation separately from a design concern: a garment may match its specification and still need a fit revision.

Review the agreed representative sizes on suitable fit references, including the range ends when required by the development plan. Observe waistband position, coverage, gusset placement and leg openings while standing and moving. Do not approve the whole range only because the middle size looks correct.

sections.title: Resolve corrections before allocating production quantities
paragraphs: If one size fails, determine whether the issue is a sample-making error or a grading rule that also affects adjacent sizes. Document which pattern points change and which samples must be resubmitted. Rechecking only the visibly problematic garment may miss a shared grading issue.

After fit and measurements are approved, record the production quantity for each model, colour and size. That commercial allocation is separate from the size-set approval. Use customer demand and replenishment plans to choose the ratio instead of treating the supplier's sample assortment as a recommended sales mix.

sections.title: Size-set questions
paragraphs: Is a size set the same as a fit sample? A base fit sample establishes the design direction in a selected size; a size set checks its translation across the agreed range. The exact development sequence should be confirmed with the supplier.
Does 2XL have a universal measurement? No. The label needs a defined body-size guide and a corresponding garment specification for the style.

Can a colour change affect an approved size set? Changes to material or finishing may affect the garment. Agree which measurements and fit checks must be repeated when the production specification changes.

description: Prepare underwear SKU codes, size-colour allocations and carton packing lists. Keep plain and printed models distinct and reconcile units before shipment.

imageCaption: M002 Print is a separate catalogue model reference. Keep the full model name in the SKU mapping so printed and plain products cannot be confused during packing.
intro: An underwear packing list should connect each carton to the exact model, colour, size and quantity inside it. Create the SKU mapping before approving labels or packing instructions, then reconcile it with the purchase order and shipment totals. DIYASI's M002 Print, DYS229 and DYS302 show why a short generic description such as underwear assortment is insufficient: different styles, materials and size-colour variants need identifiers that both the factory and receiving warehouse can follow.

sections.title: Distinguish the product model from the sellable SKU
paragraphs: A model identifies a style; a SKU identifies the unit your business manages, usually including a particular colour and size. Retain the supplier's complete model reference alongside your own code. M002 Print should remain distinct from M002, even if your internal coding system abbreviates the name.

For an illustrative internal code, D229-BLK-M could identify a proposed DYS229 black medium unit once the colour and size are confirmed. This is an example naming convention, not an existing DIYASI stock code or a barcode. Keep the mapping readable and stable across the order documents.

sections.title: Define single units, multipacks and mixed cartons
paragraphs: State whether quantity means individual garments, retail multipacks or inner packs. If a proposed three-pack contains three garments, record both pack count and garment count. Define the component colours and sizes of the pack rather than leaving the factory to infer the assortment.

Choose whether cartons contain one SKU or an agreed mixed allocation. A mixed carton needs a line for each variant inside it. Confirm the packing arrangement with the receiving warehouse, especially when it expects a specific carton label or unpacking sequence.

sections.title: Approve labels against the SKU master
paragraphs: Review label artwork with the model, colour, size and unit definition beside it. If a barcode is required, supply the authorised identifier for the sales channel and verify that the encoded value matches the intended unit. An internal SKU is not automatically a valid retail barcode identifier.

Ask for a physical or print-proof review appropriate to the packing process, then check readability and placement on the intended packaging. Keep label version control separate from the garment's size-label artwork: an accurate garment label does not guarantee an accurate outer-pack label.

sections.title: Reconcile the shipment before release
paragraphs: Compare packed quantities by SKU with the approved allocation and identify shortages, extras or substitutions explicitly. Sum garment units, inner packs and cartons using their own units. Record actual carton dimensions and weights when available; do not present early freight estimates as final packing facts.

Agree how discrepancies will be corrected and which final list accompanies the shipment. The approved order, carton labels and packing list should tell the same story. This check supports receiving accuracy; it does not replace product inspection or the commercial shipping documents required for the order.

sections.title: Packing-list questions
paragraphs: Can plain and printed products share one SKU? Keep distinct sellable variants identifiable. If they belong in one retail assortment, define the pack SKU and its exact component list.
Can I choose a size mix after labels are printed? A change may affect labels, carton allocation and quantities. Reconcile and reapprove the affected records before packing.
Does this checklist confirm a packaging service or price? No. Discuss the requested materials, labels, pack configuration, quantities and costs with the supplier for the actual order.

title: Underwear Pre-Production Sample Approval Checklist
description: Approve underwear pre-production samples with a clear version record. Check materials, measurements, construction, artwork and open corrections before release.
coverAlt: Mint green DIYASI DYS322 low-rise thong showing its smooth front panel and clean-cut edges
imageCaption: DYS322 has a polyamide-spandex body and a bonded cotton gusset. Approval of this construction requires the physical sample and agreed checks, not the front photograph alone.
intro: A pre-production sample approval should identify the exact garment version and the requirements that have been accepted before bulk production proceeds. Review materials, measurements, construction, colour, artwork and any required test evidence against the agreed specification. Record outstanding corrections and who can release them. The checklist below helps a buyer organise that decision; it is a proposed approval process, not a report that a specific DIYASI order has already passed inspection.

sections.title: Confirm what the sample represents
paragraphs: Ask whether the sample uses the proposed production fabric, trims, artwork and construction. If any component is a substitute, record it clearly and identify the later approval needed. A fit sample in a convenient colour can answer fit questions without settling the final colour or material approval.

Attach the buyer style code, supplier model, size, colour, tech-pack version and sample identifier to the review. Keep the approval tied to that physical garment and document set. A message referring only to the latest sample can become ambiguous after several revisions.

sections.title: Inspect the details that belong to the selected model
paragraphs: DYS322 is a low-rise thong with a bonded cotton gusset. Review edge finish and gusset attachment under the agreed inspection and wash plan. LS005 is a V-waist lace-and-cotton thong, so the lace join, waistband symmetry and inside finish are relevant approval points.

M005 uses a polyester-spandex body with modal pouch lining. Check the pouch construction and request the final component composition; the public catalogue does not supply exact percentages. If a recycled-polyester option is selected, include the order-specific material documentation in the approval record.

sections.title: Write decisions that cannot be mistaken for blanket approval
paragraphs: Use a clear status for each item, such as accepted, correction required or awaiting evidence. Describe the action, responsible party and verification needed to close an open item. If fit is accepted but colour is pending, say exactly that and define whether any production activity is authorised at that stage.

Avoid a general approval with unresolved comments attached. Confirm the final release in one consolidated record that references the approved sample and current documents. Retain matching references with the buyer and factory where practical so later checks use the same standard.

sections.title: Separate sample approval from production inspection
paragraphs: An approved sample establishes a reference; it does not prove that every bulk garment matches it. Agree the production and final inspection plan separately, including how measurements, workmanship, quantities and packing will be assessed and how discrepancies are handled.

If a material, pattern, colour, label or construction changes after approval, identify the affected checks and obtain the required revised approval. Keep the change log with the order. This helps avoid treating a previously approved garment as evidence for a materially different production version.

sections.title: Pre-production approval questions
paragraphs: Can photographs approve a sample? They can support visual decisions, but they cannot establish hand feel, fibre composition, fit or every inside detail. Agree when physical samples and test evidence are required.
Does sample approval also approve all sizes? Only if the approval explicitly covers the agreed size-set evidence. A single base-size sample does not verify grading across the range.

Can production start with an open correction? That depends on the specific written agreement. Identify the unresolved issue and the permitted activity clearly rather than assuming a partial approval releases the full order.

title: Cotton vs Polyamide Underwear: A Private Label Comparison
description: Compare cotton-spandex and polyamide-spandex underwear using DIYASI styles. Review fabric, edge finish, gusset and sample checks for your private-label range.
coverAlt: Blue DIYASI DYS201 low-rise cotton bikini brief with finished waist and leg edges
imageCaption: DYS201 is listed as 95% cotton and 5% spandex. Compare the actual garment with polyamide styles before choosing the material and construction for your collection.
intro: For a private-label underwear range, cotton versus polyamide is a material decision; coverage, edge finish and gusset attachment are separate choices. DIYASI's DYS201 offers a cotton-spandex bikini starting point, while DYS323 and DYS314 use polyamide-spandex bodies with cotton gussets. Choose the product requirements first, then compare finished samples. A fibre percentage alone cannot establish softness, drying speed, durability or how visible an edge will be under clothing.

sections.title: Compare the body fabric and construction separately
paragraphs: A useful supplier comparison identifies both the fibre blend and the garment construction. The current DYS201 specification lists 95% cotton and 5% spandex. DYS323 and DYS314 list an 80% polyamide and 20% spandex body with a 100% cotton gusset. These are specifications for the named models, not a rule for every cotton or polyamide product.

The three examples also have different silhouettes and finishes. DYS201 is a low-rise bikini, DYS323 a low-rise Brazilian with a bonded gusset, and DYS314 a high-waisted full brief with a stitched gusset. Comparing them can help build a range, but it does not isolate the effect of fabric: cut, tension and coverage also change the wearing experience.
rows: Low-rise bikini shape and finished waist and leg edges
Laser-cut edges and bonded gusset attachment

sections.title: Start with the buyer's intended use
paragraphs: For a cotton-led everyday collection, DYS201 provides a familiar bikini silhouette to review for fit, waistband tension and the desired hand feel. Ask for fabric weight, finish and care requirements where these are important to your brief. Two fabrics with the same cotton percentage can still differ in knit structure and finished feel.

For a collection intended to sit discreetly under fitted clothing, review the laser-cut polyamide styles on the intended wearer and under representative outer garments. Visibility depends on the edge, fit, garment colour and outer fabric together. Do not approve a universal no-show claim from the product photograph alone.

sections.title: Use the same conditions for sample comparisons
paragraphs: Record the sample size, body measurements and intended fit before comparing styles. Photograph the waist and leg openings in consistent conditions and identify where the garment presses, rolls or moves. If the purpose is to compare materials directly, ask whether comparable silhouettes can be sampled and confirm any development cost first.

Agree a wash-and-wear review appropriate to the intended care instructions. Record dimensional change, colour transfer, surface appearance and recovery; for bonded styles, also examine the bond after washing and stretching. These are proposed approval checks, not claims that a particular style has passed a specified laboratory test.

sections.title: Specify the gusset and branding as separate components
paragraphs: A cotton gusset does not make the whole garment cotton. Keep body and gusset compositions separate in the technical brief, and agree the required consumer label for the destination market. Attachment also matters: the bonded and stitched examples above need different construction reviews.

Provide the proposed logo size, placement and colour with the model number. Ask the factory to confirm a suitable application method for the actual fabric and assess the branded sample after the agreed care cycle. Do not transfer an approved logo process from one material to another without checking it.

sections.title: Common questions before choosing a fabric
paragraphs: Is cotton underwear automatically the more breathable option? Fibre content alone does not settle that comparison. Fabric weight, knit, finishes, coverage and testing conditions all matter; request evidence for any specific performance claim.
Does polyamide mean seamless? No. Polyamide names a fibre family, while seamless and no-show describe construction or intended appearance. Review the seams, edges and gusset of the selected style.

Should a first collection include both materials? Only if each serves a defined customer need. Shortlist the exact models and sizes, then confirm sample charges, colour choices and separate custom-component minimums in the quotation.

title: High-Waisted Briefs vs Thongs: Coverage & Fit for Buyers
description: Compare high-waisted briefs and thongs for your underwear range. Use DIYASI examples to review rise, rear coverage, leg openings and size-set samples.
coverAlt: Light grey DIYASI DYS219 cotton brief with a high waistband and high-cut leg openings
imageCaption: DYS219 combines a high waist with a high-cut leg. Waist height, leg shape and rear coverage should be specified separately in a buying brief.
intro: High-waisted briefs and high-waisted thongs can share a higher waistband position while offering very different rear coverage. A high leg opening is another independent feature. For wholesale and private-label selection, define rise, front and back coverage, leg opening and waistband behaviour separately. DIYASI's DYS219, DYS225 and DYS314 give buyers three different high-rise starting points to compare, without treating a high waist as a promise of compression or shaping.

sections.title: High waist, high leg and full coverage mean different things
paragraphs: High waist describes the intended waistband position. High leg describes the shape and height of the leg opening. Full coverage describes a coverage direction, particularly at the back, and still needs a visual reference and measurements. Combining these words into one label can leave the factory and buyer picturing different garments.

A high-waisted thong may provide more front coverage while retaining a narrow back. A high-leg brief may show more of the upper leg without having the same rear shape as a thong. Ask for front, back and side views of the exact model instead of making a selection from a front photograph alone.

sections.title: Compare three actual high-rise styles
paragraphs: DYS219 is listed as a high-leg cotton brief, DYS225 as a cotton high-waist thong, and DYS314 as a seamless high-waist full brief. The cotton examples list 95% cotton and 5% spandex; DYS314 lists an 80% polyamide and 20% spandex body with a cotton gusset.

The catalogue size ranges below are references for these models. They do not establish identical measurements between styles or guarantee immediate stock in every size. Confirm the current sample availability and the production measurement chart for the sizes you intend to sell.
rows: XXS, XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL

sections.title: Build the measurement sheet around coverage
paragraphs: Record finished front rise, back rise and side height using an agreed measurement method. Add waist and leg-opening measurements, gusset length and width, and marked front and back references. A request for two centimetres more coverage is ambiguous unless the drawing shows where the change belongs.

Use the intended wearer and size set to assess the waistband while standing, sitting and moving. Note rolling, pressure or movement at specific locations. A higher rise should not be treated as a correction for every fit issue; the required change may involve the waistband, body length, stretch or leg-opening shape.

sections.title: Give each silhouette a role in the assortment
paragraphs: One possible starting assortment pairs a high-rise brief for buyers seeking more rear coverage with a high-rise thong for buyers seeking a narrower back. A high-leg cotton style and a laser-cut full brief may also address different material and finishing preferences. This is a way to organise sample questions, not evidence that any combination will sell best.

Keep the first comparison manageable by using a defined colour and size reference. Once the fit is approved, plan the size and colour allocation for each model. Treat a label change, a custom colour and a new silhouette as separate requirements in the quotation, because their development work and component quantities can differ.

sections.title: Questions to resolve before placing a bulk order
paragraphs: Does high-waisted underwear count as shapewear? Not by itself. Waist position does not establish compression. Any shaping or support claim needs a defined design requirement and appropriate evidence.
Can the same size chart be used for all three styles? Do not assume so. Check the finished measurements, fit allowance and grading of each approved sample, even when the size labels match.

Can a thong be made by narrowing an existing brief? That is a development request rather than a simple name change. The back, leg opening and gusset relationship must be reviewed together, with sample work and feasibility confirmed by the factory.

title: Plain vs Printed Men's Underwear: Private Label Buying Guide
description: Plan plain and printed men's underwear for private label. Compare DIYASI models and prepare artwork, waistband, sample approval and reorder requirements.
coverAlt: DIYASI M006 Print men's trunk with a white ground and red and black all-over artwork
imageCaption: M006 Print is a separate catalogue reference from M006. The pictured artwork illustrates a printed style; custom artwork, process and quantities are confirmed for each project.
intro: For a private-label men's underwear range, plain and printed styles need different colour and artwork approvals, but both start with an approved fit. Use the complete model reference when comparing options: DIYASI's M006 and M006 Print are separate catalogue entries, not a promise of identical measurements with a different surface design. Build the order around the selected silhouette, body and pouch materials, waistband specification and an agreed sample for each colour or artwork direction.

sections.title: Choose the base garment before developing artwork
paragraphs: A plain body can put more visual emphasis on the waistband and garment shape. An all-over print adds another set of choices: motif size, repeat, orientation and how the design meets seams. Neither option is automatically easier to sell; assign each a clear role for the intended customer and price position.

M006 is a plain trunk reference, M006 Print a printed trunk, and M003 Print a printed boxer brief. Their listed materials describe a polyester-and-spandex body with modal in the gusset or pouch area. That wording does not make the full garment modal, establish the exact body blend, or verify recycled content. Confirm those details for the actual base fabric before approving labels or claims.

sections.title: What changes between plain and printed orders?
paragraphs: Separate garment fit approval from colour and artwork approval. A fit sample can establish measurements without being the final colour or print, provided that difference is recorded. The final approval should identify the actual material, appearance and construction that production must follow.

sections.title: Make the print brief reproducible
paragraphs: Provide the artwork file in a format agreed with the factory, its version, intended repeat dimensions, colour references and direction. State whether the design repeats across the fabric or must sit in a specific position on the garment. Supply artwork you own or are authorised to use.

Ask the factory to confirm the print method for the selected fabric; a catalogue photograph does not establish the manufacturing process. Review a print trial on the intended substrate, then check the assembled sample for motif scale, stretching and placement near the pouch and seams. Agree any matching requirement before the quote, because it can affect cutting and material use.

sections.title: Approve the waistband and care performance separately
paragraphs: The waistband is a separate component even when its colour or graphics coordinate with the body. Specify width, logo repeat, artwork orientation, attachment and the intended colour relationship. Keep its approved reference with the garment sample rather than treating a logo file as full waistband approval.

Agree the relevant wash, colour-transfer and stretch checks for the finished product. Record what will be assessed and which sample represents production. Neither a printed appearance nor the fibre names establish colourfastness, stretch recovery or a tested performance level.

sections.title: Plan quantities and reorders by colourway
paragraphs: An order total can hide small quantities across many sizes and artworks. Prepare a matrix that shows the pieces for each model, size and colourway, then ask which garment, fabric, printing and waistband minimums apply. Do not assume a catalogue garment minimum covers every custom component.

For repeat orders, retain the approved artwork version, fabric specification, colour reference, finished measurements and sample approval record. Review size-level sales and remaining stock before repeating the same allocation. A matching model number alone is not enough to reproduce an earlier custom order.

sections.title: Common questions about custom printed underwear
paragraphs: Is printed underwear always more expensive? Not necessarily. Cost depends on the base fabric, artwork, process, setup and quantity. Compare quotations using the same specification and ask for development and production costs to be separated.

Can a printed style use the fit approved for a plain style? Ask the factory to confirm the pattern and material relationship. In this catalogue, M006 and M006 Print are distinct products, so compare measurements before assuming equivalence.

Can a brand launch with one plain and one printed style? Yes, that is a possible assortment plan, subject to feasibility and quantities. Keep the fit, branding and artwork approvals distinct so each part of the order has a clear production reference.

title: DIYASI Underwear Catalogue: Styles, Sizes & Sample Planning
description: Explore the refreshed DIYASI catalogue, with original photographs, style comparisons and size references for wholesale and private-label buyers.
coverAlt: Production workspace at the DIYASI underwear factory
imageCaption: A view of the DIYASI production workspace. Product specifications and order requirements are confirmed separately for each project.
intro: The refreshed DIYASI website brings 45 underwear styles into one catalogue for buyers developing a wholesale or private-label collection. Original product photography, individual style information and comparison tools make it easier to prepare a shortlist before discussing samples.

sections.title: Explore a collection, then review the individual style
paragraphs: Women's collections include cotton-rich underwear, lace-trimmed silhouettes and no-show styles in stretch polyamide. The men's range includes briefs, trunks and boxer briefs. Collection pages offer a starting point; each product page gives the model number, stated fabric composition, size range and original photographs.

A collection name does not describe every construction detail. For example, buyers comparing no-show underwear should still check the edge finish and gusset attachment on the selected model. Keeping the model number in a sample request helps the team discuss the same garment.

sections.title: Keep the original details in view
paragraphs: The product gallery displays the original photographs in full, so branding and construction details remain visible. Each style also has a size-guide image from the source catalogue. These references support the first conversation; the final measurement chart and tolerances still need agreement for the intended market.

Buyers can compare up to four styles while considering fabric, fit, size range and order information. A useful shortlist might include a cotton everyday option, a lace-trimmed alternative and a no-show style, with a clear reason for sampling each one.

sections.title: Turn a shortlist into a sample brief
paragraphs: When contacting DIYASI, include the selected model numbers, target market, approximate quantity and any proposed changes to colours, branding or packaging. Note whether the existing silhouette will be retained or whether a new fit is required.

Most current catalogue specification tables list a starting quantity of 120 pieces per style, with mixed sizes and colours subject to confirmation. That reference does not establish a minimum for custom fabric, labels, waistbands or packaging. Sample charges and production timing are confirmed against the actual brief.

The sourcing guides explain how to prepare quotations, review gussets and organise sample approvals. News and insights will add collection notes and company updates as there is useful information to share.

title: Bikini vs Brazilian Underwear: Coverage & Fit Compared
description: Compare bikini and Brazilian underwear using actual DIYASI cotton, lace and no-show styles. Build a sample brief around coverage, rise and construction.
coverAlt: DIYASI LS006 cotton Brazilian brief with lace waistband and leg openings
imageCaption: LS006 is a cotton-and-lace Brazilian style. Its construction is one example within the category, not a specification for every Brazilian brief.
intro: Bikini and Brazilian describe a direction for the silhouette, but the name alone is not enough to approve a product. For a buying decision, compare the actual front and back coverage, rise, side width and leg opening on the selected garments. Then review the fabric and finishing details independently.

sections.title: Use the back view as part of the brief
paragraphs: A Brazilian cut generally provides less rear coverage than a conventional bikini, although the exact shape varies between designs and suppliers. A front photograph can hide much of that difference. Include front and back references when requesting samples and identify the areas where more or less coverage is intended.

Rise is a separate choice. A lower waistband does not automatically mean a narrower back, and a higher waistband does not establish how the leg opening will sit. Record the intended rise and coverage as separate points rather than relying on one category label.

sections.title: Compare the construction as well as the cut
paragraphs: The DIYASI catalogue provides several useful starting points. DYS201 is a bikini with a stated body composition of 95% cotton and 5% spandex. LS006 is a Brazilian brief with a 95% cotton and 5% spandex body, plus polyamide-and-spandex lace. DYS323 is also a Brazilian style, but its body is listed as 80% polyamide and 20% spandex with a cotton gusset.

This comparison separates silhouette from material. Two Brazilian briefs can use different edges, fabrics and gusset construction. Neither the name nor the fibre percentage proves how a garment will feel on a particular wearer or perform after repeated washing. Confirm those requirements through an appropriate sample review and supporting tests where needed.

sections.title: Give each sample a clear purpose
paragraphs: For an initial range, a buyer might sample one bikini and one Brazilian to compare coverage, then decide whether an additional lace or no-show construction serves a different customer need. This is a planning option rather than a fixed recommendation for every brand.

Use the same measurement method and record the size worn for each comparison. Note any requested adjustments with marked photographs or a measurement sheet. Before asking for a production quote, identify which model and construction have been selected, which details stay unchanged and which need development. Final size allocation, colours and component quantities should be confirmed with the factory.

title: Trunks vs Boxer Briefs: Inseam, Fit & Sourcing Guide
description: A buyer's comparison of men's trunks and boxer briefs, covering inseam, fit, pouch materials and waistband details with real DIYASI style references.
coverAlt: DIYASI M006 men's trunk with a branded waistband
imageCaption: M006 is listed as a trunk in the DIYASI catalogue. Confirm the finished inseam and other measurements for your selected size.
intro: The practical starting point for choosing between trunks and boxer briefs is the intended leg length and fit. Category names vary, so a sourcing brief should specify the finished inseam, leg opening, rise and waistband rather than asking for a silhouette by name alone.

sections.title: Turn the silhouette into measurable details
paragraphs: Trunks usually describe a shorter leg, while boxer briefs generally extend further down the thigh. There is no single inseam that every supplier uses for those names. Request measurements for the actual model and sample size, and agree where each measurement begins and ends.

The DIYASI catalogue includes M006 as a trunk, M007 as a boxer brief and M002 as a long-leg boxer. These give buyers different starting silhouettes to discuss. Their category descriptions are not a substitute for an approved size chart or a fit assessment.
rows: Why it belongs in the sample brief
Makes the intended leg length explicit for each size
Defines the finished opening alongside the chosen fabric and construction
Records the intended waistband position and body coverage
Identifies width, artwork, attachment and approved sample reference

sections.title: Keep body and pouch materials separate
paragraphs: The source specifications for M006 and M007 describe a polyester-and-spandex body with modal in the gusset or pouch area. That does not make the whole garment modal. When comparing suppliers, ask for the body, pouch or gusset, waistband and other components to be identified separately.

The same composition description can still leave important details open, including the fabric weight, knit structure, finish and exact blend. Request those details where they affect the intended product. Claims about moisture handling, support, durability or reduced rubbing need suitable evidence; they should not be inferred from the silhouette or a fibre name.

sections.title: Review fit before committing to the assortment
paragraphs: Start a sample comparison with a consistent size reference and record the wearer's observations about the waistband, pouch and legs. If a sample rides up or feels restrictive, describe the location and conditions rather than assuming that changing the category name will solve it. The production team can then assess the relevant measurement, material or construction.

Once the fit direction is chosen, agree the size grading, colour allocation and waistband artwork. Printed and plain styles should be identified by their exact model reference, because similar model names can describe different products in a catalogue. Confirm sample charges, component minimums and production milestones in the written quotation.
